What this is gets four answers, and everything else follows from them. Gill reads the night as the darkness of the Old Testament church under the shadow of the ceremonial law, Christ's absence making night as his presence makes day. Henry takes the same allegory and gives it a history: it was hard for that church to find Christ in the types and figures, and the consolation of Israel was long looked for before an old man held him in his arms at last. Wesley reads throughout of Christ's presence sought and withdrawn. Clarke keeps it literal, supposing the bridegroom came only by night and on this occasion did not come as usual. Ellicott treats it as a poem, a reminiscence of their love before the marriage, put by the writer into his lady's mouth.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the fourth reading, that she is relating a dream, and use it to solve a difficulty the others leave standing. On any outward account the question she puts to the night watch is foolish, since there is no reason they should know her beloved; but in a dream feeling and imagination rise higher than reflection, and things follow quickly without fixed outlines. They also make the pain recur: the sense of being forgotten returns for several nights together, until she grows distrustful of his fidelity, and the more she fears she is no longer loved the more ardent her longing becomes. Gill notices the same plural, one night after another, taking it for constancy in seeking rather than recurring doubt.

Why the first search failed is answered by fault rather than by circumstance. Henry is hardest on her: it was late and lazy seeking, her understanding clouded because it was by night, her affections chilled because it was on her bed and half asleep, like the virgins who slumbered while the bridegroom stayed away. Wesley offers two reasons for the withdrawal, that she had not sought him diligently or that she had abused his favour, and chooses neither. Gill has her perceive she had taken a wrong method and leave her bed of sloth at once. Wesley marks the search moving outward, from private prayer to the places of public assembly.

The watchmen are read as officers of two quite different cities. Gill and Wesley both make them ministers of the gospel, called watchmen as the prophets were, whose business is to give the time of night, declare the state of the church and warn of danger. Ellicott instead quotes a modern traveller on an eastern city after dark, where the streets are deserted and the guard creeps softly about and arrests anyone found walking without a light. Wesley adds the two shrewdest observations here: she does not name the man she seeks, thinking it needless that anyone in such an office could fail to know him, and their answer goes unrecorded either because it was no answer or because their silence told her they could not help.

Where she takes him when she finds him is read literally by one and figuratively by the rest. Clarke explains that eastern women have separate apartments no one but the husband enters, compares a patriarch bringing his bride into his mother's tent, and concludes that this belongs to the third night of the wedding. Wesley makes the mother the universal church, the Jerusalem above which is the mother of us all, into which believers bring Christ by faith and prayer. Ellicott reports without adopting it an older tradition that read the holding fast as a prophecy of the woman at the tomb on the resurrection morning. Keil and Delitzsch, pressing their dream, doubt the daughters of Jerusalem are present at all, and have her deprecating any disturbance of the ecstasy while pointing towards a city still distant.
6:
The question opening the second half is agreed to come from the women of the city, and disagreed about in every other respect. Gill, Henry and Wesley take the person admired to be the bride, though Clarke reports some understand the bridegroom. On the wilderness Gill offers a state of nature before conversion, barren and full of perplexing tracks; Wesley makes it the Gentile world out of which believers are called, and hears in the pillars of smoke the cloud that led Israel. Henry gives three applications: the nation coming up after forty years of wandering, any public deliverance of the church, and the recovery of a single soul out of desertion. Ellicott declines all of it and defines the word as open country, the land of nomads against that of settled people.

Ellicott's frame for the pageant is the most distinctive thing here. He takes the scene as passing only in the theatre of the fancy, introduced into the marriage song partly from sympathy with newly wedded people and partly to set the simplicity of his own espousals, where the joy centred wholly in true love, against the pomp of a royal marriage which was a state ceremony. On his reading the royal procession is a foil, not the subject. Clarke stays with the literal wedding: going to Egypt was called descending and coming from it coming up, the clouds of incense around the litter seemed like pillars of smoke, and with this verse the third night ends. Ellicott adds that heading a procession with incense is an ancient eastern custom, probably a relic of ceremonies in which gods were carried.

The bed and its guard are read as figures of security, Gill making it the church visible, Christ's resting place. Henry notices that the name Solomon occurs three times here and only three times besides in the whole song, and builds on its meaning peace: Christ's bed, though he had nowhere to lay his head, is better than Solomon's best, being the church, the hearts of believers, heaven, and the rest gracious souls find in communion with him. On the sixty armed men he draws the distinction the passage turns on: those who rest in Christ not only dwell at ease, as many do who are in the greatest danger, but dwell in safety, their holy serenity under the protection of a holy security.

The word for what the king made occurs nowhere else, and the three who work on it reach three positions. Gill lays out the possibilities: a bride chamber, a nuptial bed carried from place to place, the open chariot in which a bride was brought from her father's house, the ancient litter resembling a sedan, or the vehicle in which three rode together, the bride between the bridegroom and his friend. Clarke judges it very likely that a nuptial bed and not a chariot is meant, allowing it may be a palanquin. Ellicott traces the etymology through four languages and concludes firmly for a palanquin, on two grounds: the context describes the approach of a royal procession, and the word rendered covering suits a movable litter rather than a bed of state.

Wesley alone allegorises the vehicle, making it the word of Christ dispensed by his ministers, in which he rides triumphantly and believers are carried to glory, and finding in the incorruptible cedar a word that endures for ever. Gill treats the silver pillars the same way, as the doctrines of the gospel, solid and substantial and worth more than thousands of gold and silver. Clarke keeps to furniture, comparing the silver bedposts to plated chairs in a royal apartment. Keil and Delitzsch close the scene by distinguishing the two groups of women, those of Jerusalem being the court, and have the call go to the city at large to see the king as the procession approaches.
